Reading route

The numbered sections follow the slides in the same order, and each slide links to its section here. The notebook adds the R output and the explanations for study after class.

  1. From SES to Holt: what Session 16 left us with, and what changes today.
  2. Holt’s linear trend: the SES equations with a slope added.
  3. SES and Holt in R: fit both, compare their forecasts, inspect Holt’s states.
  4. Reading the equations: predict first, then update; what \(\beta^*\) does to the slope.
  5. Holt by hand: one update on a calculator, then the Excel workbook.
  6. Damped trend: the equations with \(\phi\) added, the fitted damped model, how \(\phi\) flattens the forecast, and what small and large values of \(\alpha\), \(\beta^*\) and \(\phi\) mean.
  7. Judge the forecasts: what a forecast’s shape can and cannot tell us.

The required work is workbook 17_B, the calculator check and Exercise 1, including its damped forecast check. The appendix holds optional material: a reconstruction of the fitted values, the algebra behind the damped forecast limit, custom bounds for \(\phi\), reference sketches and optional cross-validation.

1. From SES to Holt

Last session. In Session 16 on fitting SES, a search chose the smoothing weight \(\alpha\) and the initial level \(\ell_0\) by making the one-step training errors small. We then checked the forecasts on later observations, and saw that a better training fit does not guarantee better forecasts.

Today. SES keeps one state, the level, so its forecast is flat: \(\hat y_{T+h|T}=\ell_T\) at every horizon. No choice of \(\alpha\) can tilt it. Today we add a second state, a slope, which gives Holt’s linear trend method, and then a damping factor that flattens that slope at long horizons.

Session 16: SES Today: Holt and damped Holt
States level \(\ell_t\) level \(\ell_t\) and slope \(b_t\)
Forecast shape flat line at \(\ell_T\) straight line \(\ell_T+hb_T\); damped: a line that flattens
Weights \(\alpha\) \(\alpha\) and \(\beta^*\); damped adds \(\phi\)
How they are fitted search for the smallest training SSE the same search, with more values to choose

The Australian population series shows why the slope matters. The global_economy dataset records population annually from 1960 to 2017; dividing Population by a million gives Pop, in millions.

aus_economy <- global_economy |>
  filter(Code == "AUS") |>
  mutate(Pop = Population / 1e6)

autoplot(aus_economy, Pop) +
  labs(y = "Millions", title = "Australian population")

Population rises every year in this sample. A forecast that stays flat at the 2017 value cannot be right for long.

2. Holt’s linear trend

The SES equations with a slope added

Start from the SES equations of Session 15 and add what Holt needs. The terms in color are new:

\[ \begin{align*} \text{SES}\qquad &\text{Forecast} && \hat y_{t+h|t}=\ell_t\\ &\text{Level} && \ell_t=\alpha y_t+(1-\alpha)\,\ell_{t-1}\\[1.2em] \text{Holt}\qquad &\text{Forecast} && \hat y_{t+h|t}=\ell_t\textcolor{#B5471E}{{}+hb_t}\\ &\text{Level} && \ell_t=\alpha y_t+(1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1}\textcolor{#B5471E}{{}+b_{t-1}})\\ &\textcolor{#B5471E}{\text{Slope}} && \textcolor{#B5471E}{b_t=\beta^*(\ell_t-\ell_{t-1})+(1-\beta^*)\,b_{t-1}} \end{align*} \]

Three changes, one idea:

  • Forecast. Each step ahead adds one more copy of the final slope, so the forecast \(\hat y_{T+h|T}=\ell_T+hb_T\) is a straight line. The slope is in the series’ units per period: here, millions of people per year.
  • Level. SES blends the new observation with the old level. Holt blends it with the old level plus one slope, because that is where Holt expected the series to be this period.
  • Slope. A new equation keeps the slope up to date. It blends the latest change in level, \(\ell_t-\ell_{t-1}\), with the previous slope. The weight \(\beta^*\), between zero and one, decides how much the slope reacts.

Unlike the drift method from Session 8 on benchmark methods, whose slope is the average change over the whole sample, Holt’s slope is revised every period. Section 4 looks at the equations in detail; first we see what they do to a forecast.

3. SES and Holt in R

Fit both and compare the forecasts

In ETS(), trend("N") gives SES and trend("A"), an additive trend, gives Holt. Both models go in one model table so that their forecasts can be plotted together:

fit_ses_holt <- aus_economy |>
  model(
    SES  = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") + trend("N") + season("N")),
    Holt = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("N"))
  )

fc_ses_holt <- fit_ses_holt |> forecast(h = 10)

fc_ses_holt |>
  autoplot(aus_economy, level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "SES stays flat; Holt continues the trend",
       y = "Population (millions)") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Forecast"))

SES forecasts 24.60 million for 2018 and every later year. Holt starts from almost the same level and adds about 0.37 million a year, reaching 28.29 million in 2027. Prediction intervals are left out to keep the two paths visible.

Inspect the Holt fit

We keep the Holt model on its own for the rest of the example:

fit <- fit_ses_holt |> select(Holt)

tidy() returns the fitted parameters: the two weights and the two initial states.

tidy(fit)
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  .model term  estimate
  <chr>  <chr>    <dbl>
1 Holt   alpha    1.000
2 Holt   beta     0.327
3 Holt   l[0]    10.1  
4 Holt   b[0]     0.222

fable reports a beta that is \(\alpha\beta^*\), not the \(\beta^*\) of the equations and the workbook. Divide by alpha to recover \(\beta^*\). holt_estimates$term == "alpha" marks the row whose term is alpha, and holt_estimates$estimate[...] takes the estimate on that row:

holt_estimates <- tidy(fit)
alpha_hat <- holt_estimates$estimate[holt_estimates$term == "alpha"]
beta_hat <- holt_estimates$estimate[holt_estimates$term == "beta"]

# beta-star, the slope weight in the equations and the workbook
beta_hat / alpha_hat
[1] 0.3266692

Here alpha is 0.9999, so beta and \(\beta^*\) agree to three decimals, 0.327. In Session 18 on Holt-Winters alpha is far from one, and the two differ.

NoteParameterization reference: beta and beta-star

Substitute the level’s error-correction form, \(\ell_t=\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1}+\alpha e_t\) (section 4), into the slope update:

\[ b_t=b_{t-1}+\alpha\beta^* e_t=b_{t-1}+\beta e_t, \qquad \beta=\alpha\beta^*. \]

These are two parameterizations of the same update. The workbook uses \(\beta^*\); tidy() reports \(\beta\).

components() returns the level and slope for every year. Note the extra year, 1959, for \(t=0\), which holds \(\ell_0\) and \(b_0\).

holts_components <- fit |> components()
holts_components
# A dable: 59 x 6 [1Y]
# Key:     .model [1]
# :        Pop = lag(level, 1) + lag(slope, 1) + remainder
   .model  Year   Pop level slope remainder
   <chr>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Holt    1959  NA    10.1 0.222 NA       
 2 Holt    1960  10.3  10.3 0.222 -0.000145
 3 Holt    1961  10.5  10.5 0.217 -0.0159

The level follows the population closely, because alpha is almost one. The slope moves between about 0.18 and 0.37 million a year: it was revised as growth sped up and slowed down.

The forecast uses only the last row. Adding one, two and three final slopes to the final level reproduces forecast() for 2018 to 2020. tail(holts_components, 1) keeps the last row and pull(.mean) extracts the point forecasts as plain numbers:

final <- tail(holts_components, 1)
final$level + (1:3) * final$slope
[1] 24.96786 25.33678 25.70571
fc_ses_holt |> filter(.model == "Holt") |> head(3) |> pull(.mean)
[1] 24.96786 25.33678 25.70571

4. Reading the equations

Predict first, then update

Before \(y_t\) arrives, Holt predicts it from the states it already has:

\[ \hat y_{t|t-1}=\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1}. \]

This is the prior prediction of \(y_t\): prior because it is made before \(y_t\) is observed, from the states at \(t-1\). It is the forecast rule at horizon one, made one period earlier. fable calls it the fitted value (the .fitted column of augment()), and the workbook heads its column Fitted Value. The three names refer to the same number.

Each period then runs in a fixed order:

  1. Predict \(y_t\): \(\hat y_{t|t-1}=\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1}\), before seeing \(y_t\).
  2. Update the level: \(\ell_t=\alpha y_t+(1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1})\), a blend of what we saw and what we predicted.
  3. Update the slope: \(b_t=\beta^*(\ell_t-\ell_{t-1})+(1-\beta^*)b_{t-1}\), using the new level.
  4. Predict \(y_{t+1}\): \(\hat y_{t+1|t}=\ell_t+b_t\), from the new level and the new slope. When \(y_{t+1}\) arrives, the cycle repeats from step 1.

The figure draws one period with schematic numbers, step by step. Start at \(t-1\) with the observation \(y_{t-1}\) and the level \(\ell_{t-1}\) and slope \(b_{t-1}\) after it.

The level update can also be read as a correction: \(\ell_t=(\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1})+\alpha e_t\), where \(e_t=y_t-\hat y_{t|t-1}\) is the prediction error. The level moves a fraction \(\alpha\) of the way from the prediction toward the observation.

The latest change in level, \(\ell_t-\ell_{t-1}\), is a one-period estimate of the slope: the rise over a run of one period. The slope update averages that fresh estimate with the slope carried from before, so the new slope always lies between the two. In the figure, all three are drawn over the same period, from \(t-1\) to \(t\): the dashed old slope, the thin line from \(\ell_{t-1}\) to \(\ell_t\), and the new slope between them. After that the old slope is no longer used: step 4 needs only \(\ell_t\) and \(b_t\), which is why the line to \(y_{t+1}\) is parallel to the new slope.

What \(\beta^*\) does to the slope

\(\beta^*\) is not the slope. It is the weight that decides how fast the slope reacts to changes in the level. To see it, hold \(\alpha\) at 0.8 and fix \(\beta^*\) at three values. In fable the weights can be fixed inside trend(); remember that its beta is \(\alpha\beta^*\):

alpha_demo <- 0.8

fit_beta <- aus_economy |>
  model(
    `beta* = 0.05` = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") +
                           trend("A", alpha = alpha_demo, beta = alpha_demo * 0.05) +
                           season("N")),
    `beta* = 0.3`  = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") +
                           trend("A", alpha = alpha_demo, beta = alpha_demo * 0.3) +
                           season("N")),
    `beta* = 0.9`  = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") +
                           trend("A", alpha = alpha_demo, beta = alpha_demo * 0.9) +
                           season("N"))
  )

The slope component of each fit shows the difference:

fit_beta |>
  components() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Year, y = slope, colour = .model)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Small beta-star: a steady slope. Large beta-star: a jumpy one",
       y = "Slope (millions per year)", colour = "Model")
  • With \(\beta^*=0.05\) the slope barely moves: it behaves almost like the fixed slope of the drift method.
  • With \(\beta^*=0.9\) the slope chases every change in yearly growth, up to 0.44 in 2009 and down again two years later.
  • With \(\beta^*=0.3\) it follows the lasting changes, such as faster growth after 2005, without most of the jumps.

The training errors tell us which of the three fits the observed years best:

fit_beta |> accuracy() |> select(.model, RMSE)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  .model         RMSE
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 beta* = 0.05 0.0815
2 beta* = 0.3  0.0649
3 beta* = 0.9  0.0666

Both extremes fit worse than the middle value. A slope that never moves misses the faster growth after 2005; a slope that chases every change carries one year’s jump into the next prediction. The final slopes differ too, so the forecasts do:

fit_beta |>
  forecast(h = 10) |>
  autoplot(aus_economy, level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Forecasts from the three slope weights",
       y = "Population (millions)", colour = "Model")

Fitting: the same search as SES

ETS() chooses \(\alpha\), \(\beta^*\), \(\ell_0\) and \(b_0\) with the search from Session 16 on fitting SES, with two more values to choose. For each candidate it runs the predict-and-update cycle through the training years and adds up the squared prediction errors, the SSE. It keeps trying candidates until the SSE stops falling noticeably. Free to move both weights, it settled on \(\alpha=0.9999\) and \(\beta^*=0.327\) for the population series. augment() gives the prediction errors of that fit, so we can compute the SSE at which the search stopped:

fitted_vals <- fit |> augment()

# Sum of squared residuals
SSE <- sum(fitted_vals$.innov^2)
SSE
[1] 0.2231852

.innov holds the innovation residuals from Session 9 on residual diagnostics; for additive errors they equal .resid, the observation minus the prior prediction. As in Session 16, the smallest training SSE describes the fit to the years already seen, not the accuracy of future forecasts.

5. Holt by hand

Worked example: one update

Take a previous level \(\ell_{t-1}=80\), a previous slope \(b_{t-1}=2\) and a new observation \(y_t=86\), with \(\alpha=0.5\) and \(\beta^*=0.3\). Predict \(y_t\), update the level, update the slope, then predict \(y_{t+1}\) and \(y_{t+2}\): the steps of the list above. Commit to your numbers before opening.

TipWorked example: open after trying it
Step Formula Plug in
Predict \(y_t\) \(\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{\hat y_{t\mid t-1}}=\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{\ell_{t-1}}+\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{b_{t-1}}\) \(\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{80}+\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{2}=\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{82}\)
Update the level \(\textcolor{#B5471E}{\ell_t}=\alpha y_t+(1-\alpha)(\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{\ell_{t-1}}+\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{b_{t-1}})\) \(0.5\times86+0.5\times(\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{80}+\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{2})=\textcolor{#B5471E}{84}\)
Update the slope \(\textcolor{#B5471E}{b_t}=\beta^*(\textcolor{#B5471E}{\ell_t}-\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{\ell_{t-1}})+(1-\beta^*)\,\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{b_{t-1}}\) \(0.3\times(\textcolor{#B5471E}{84}-\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{80})+0.7\times\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{2}=\textcolor{#B5471E}{2.6}\)
Predict \(y_{t+1}\) and \(y_{t+2}\) \(\textcolor{#B5471E}{\hat y_{t+h\mid t}}=\textcolor{#B5471E}{\ell_t}+h\,\textcolor{#B5471E}{b_t}\) \(\textcolor{#B5471E}{84}+\textcolor{#B5471E}{2.6}=\textcolor{#B5471E}{86.6}\); \(\textcolor{#B5471E}{84}+2\times\textcolor{#B5471E}{2.6}=\textcolor{#B5471E}{89.2}\)

The slope update uses the updated level, 84, and the previous level, 80. The last row is what the updates are for: predictions of the next observations from the updated level and slope.

The colors are the slides’: slate before the update (the previous level and slope and the prediction of \(y_t\)), black the observation, orange after the update (the updated level and slope and their predictions). The figure puts the same update on an illustrative series with values for \(y\) over time, in the same colors, and names each forecast line by the origin it was made from. The slate dashed line is the forecast made at \(t-1\) from level 80 and slope 2: \(80+2h\), which is 82 for \(y_t\) and 84, 86 and 88 for the next three periods. The observation, 86, is 4 above the prediction. Updating the level to 84 alone would lift that line by 2, to 86, 88 and 90 (the faint line, still with slope 2). Updating the slope to 2.6 then turns it: the forecasts made at \(t\) are \(84+2.6h\), which is 86.6, 89.2 and 91.8. Workbook 17_B repeats this step once per year of the population series.

Calculator check: a changing trend

This is part of the homework. Try the same steps on new numbers. A weekly orders model has previous level 120, previous slope 3, and a new observation of 132. Use \(\alpha=0.4\) and \(\beta^*=0.25\).

  1. Predict this week’s orders (the prior prediction), then update the level and the slope.
  2. Predict the orders two weeks ahead from the updated level and slope, using Holt’s forecast rule.
  3. Explain which quantity could be used to assess the error for the newly observed week, and why.

Keep intermediate precision and round final answers to two decimals. This short check makes both weights visible; the workbook’s alpha is almost one.

Australian population workbook

The workbook 17_B in this session folder repeats the worked example in every row, for the population series. Its Fitted Value column holds the prior predictions. Predict from the previous row, update the level, then use that new level to update the slope. Filling the observation rows and ten forecasts is part of the homework.

The workbook supplies the fitted settings from section 3, rounded: \(\hat{\alpha} = 0.9999\), \(\hat{\beta}^* = 0.3267\), \(\ell_0 = 10.05\) and \(b_0 = 0.22\). Filling in the rows applies them; it does not estimate them. Rounding the initial states can change the last displayed digit (for example, 10.05 + 0.22 = 10.27). 6. Damped trend

The Holt equations with damping added

Holt extends the final slope forever, which is a strong assumption for a ten- or twenty-year forecast. The damped trend method adds a factor \(\phi\), between zero and one, that shrinks the slope a little more at every step. Start from Holt; the terms in color are new:

\[ \begin{align*} &\text{Forecast} && \hat y_{t+h|t}=\ell_t+\textcolor{#B5471E}{(\phi+\phi^2+\cdots+\phi^h)}\,b_t\\ &\text{Level} && \ell_t=\alpha y_t+(1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1}+\textcolor{#B5471E}{\phi}\, b_{t-1})\\ &\text{Slope} && b_t=\beta^*(\ell_t-\ell_{t-1})+(1-\beta^*)\,\textcolor{#B5471E}{\phi}\, b_{t-1} \end{align*} \]

  • Forecast. Holt adds \(h\) full slopes. The damped method adds \(\phi\) of the slope for the first step, \(\phi^2\) for the second, and so on, so each step adds less than the one before.
  • Updates. Whenever the slope is carried one period forward, it is multiplied by \(\phi\).
  • Two endpoints. With \(\phi=1\) every factor is one and we are back to Holt. The smaller \(\phi\), the sooner the forecast flattens.

In practice \(\phi\) is rarely below 0.8, where the damping is very strong, and rarely above 0.98, where the method is almost undamped.

Damped example: ETS() estimates \(\phi\)

trend("Ad") asks ETS() for a damped additive trend. By default it estimates \(\phi\) with the other parameters, between 0.8 and 0.98. For additive errors that is the same as minimizing the SSE; Session 19 on ETS estimation and model selection explains why. The model table holds Holt’s model next to the damped one, so that their forecasts can be compared:

fit_damped <-
  aus_economy |>
      model(
        holts = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("N")),
        damped_holts = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("N"))
      )
tidy(fit_damped)
# A tibble: 9 × 4
  Country   .model       term  estimate
  <fct>     <chr>        <chr>    <dbl>
1 Australia holts        alpha    1.000
2 Australia holts        beta     0.327
3 Australia holts        l[0]    10.1  
4 Australia holts        b[0]     0.222
5 Australia damped_holts alpha    0.999
6 Australia damped_holts beta     0.427
7 Australia damped_holts phi      0.980
8 Australia damped_holts l[0]    10.0  
9 Australia damped_holts b[0]     0.248

The estimate, \(\phi=0.98\), is the upper end of the default range: the data favor an almost undamped trend, and the bound keeps a little damping. Fifteen years ahead is enough to see the paths separate:

fc_damped <-
  fit_damped |>
  forecast(h = 15)

fc_damped |>
  autoplot(aus_economy, level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Australian population",
       y = "Millions") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Forecast"))

A table comparing the forecasts of both models:

fc_damped |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Year, .model, .mean) |>
  pivot_wider(values_from = c(`.mean`), names_from = c(`.model`))

The two paths agree to one decimal for the first two years; by 2032 the damped model forecasts 29.2 million against Holt’s 30.1.

How \(\phi\) shapes the forecast

trend("Ad", phi = ...) fixes \(\phi\) instead of estimating it. Fitting three fixed values next to Holt, and forecasting thirty years ahead, shows what the factor does:

fit_phi <- aus_economy |>
  model(
    Holt         = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("N")),
    `phi = 0.98` = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") + trend("Ad", phi = 0.98) + season("N")),
    `phi = 0.9`  = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") + trend("Ad", phi = 0.9) + season("N")),
    `phi = 0.8`  = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") + trend("Ad", phi = 0.8) + season("N"))
  )

fc_phi <- fit_phi |> forecast(h = 30)

fc_phi |>
  autoplot(aus_economy, level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The smaller phi, the sooner the forecast levels off",
       y = "Population (millions)", colour = "Model")

The four fits end with almost the same final level and slope, so the differences come from \(\phi\):

fit_phi |> components() |> as_tibble() |> group_by(.model) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1) |> select(.model, level, slope)
# A tibble: 4 × 3
# Groups:   .model [4]
  .model     level slope
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>
1 Holt        24.6 0.369
2 phi = 0.8   24.6 0.388
3 phi = 0.9   24.6 0.381
4 phi = 0.98  24.6 0.363

Each damped forecast levels off. The weights \(\phi+\phi^2+\cdots\) add up to less and less with each step, and their total approaches \(\phi/(1-\phi)\). The forecast therefore approaches

\[ \ell_T+\frac{\phi}{1-\phi}\,b_T . \]

With \(\phi=0.8\) the slope can add at most four final slopes, \(0.8/0.2=4\): \(24.60+4\times0.388\approx26.15\) million, which the forecast all but reaches within about fifteen years. With \(\phi=0.9\) the ceiling is nine slopes, \(24.59+9\times0.381\approx28.0\) million, approached more slowly. With \(\phi=0.98\) it is 49 slopes, about \(24.60+49\times0.363\approx42.4\) million, far beyond this plot: in 2047 the forecast is 32.7 million and still rising by about 0.2 million a year. A forecast at a given horizon is not the same as the limit it approaches. The appendix shows the algebra.

Check: damping a falling trend

Hold the final states at \(\ell_T=50\) and \(b_T=-2\), and take \(\phi=0.9\). At \(h=3\), is the damped forecast above or below Holt’s? Commit before opening.

TipWorked answer: open after you have committed

Holt’s forecast adds three full slopes: \(\ell_T+3b_T=50-3\times2=44\).

The damped forecast adds three shrinking ones: \(\ell_T+(\phi+\phi^2+\phi^3)b_T=50-(0.9+0.81+0.729)\times2=45.12\).

The damped forecast is above Holt’s. Damping shrinks the trend’s contribution whatever its sign, so, holding the final states fixed, it lowers a rising path and raises a falling one. Separately fitted models may have different final states as well as different damping, so compare their actual forecasts.

The three dials: what small and large values mean

Each weight is a dial that sets how a state reacts to new data. None of them is the level, the slope or the forecast itself.

Dial Small Large
\(\alpha\), the level The level stays close to its one-step projection, \(\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1}\) in Holt or \(\ell_{t-1}+\phi b_{t-1}\) with damping: a surprise barely moves it. The level follows the latest observation; at \(\alpha=1\) it is the latest observation.
\(\beta^*\), the slope The slope barely changes. In undamped Holt the trend is then almost a fixed straight line, and at \(\beta^*=0\) the slope stays at \(b_0\) for ever. In the damped method, \(\beta^*=0\) gives \(b_t=\phi b_{t-1}\), so the slope still decays when \(0<\phi<1\). The slope chases each latest change in level, so the trend can turn quickly, including on a one-off jump.
\(\phi\), the damping The slope fades fast and the forecast levels off within a few periods: with \(\phi=0.8\) it adds at most four more slopes. The slope persists and the forecast is almost Holt’s straight line; \(\phi=1\) is Holt.

The two population fits are separate models, so read each from its own rows of tidy(). The Holt fit has \(\alpha=1.00\) and \(\beta^*\approx0.33\): a level that tracks each year’s population and a slope that follows lasting changes in growth. The damped fit has \(\alpha=1.00\), \(\beta^*\approx0.43\) and \(\phi=0.98\): a slightly more responsive slope that fades only slowly. These settings describe how the method reacts; they come from the training fit, and only forecasts of later observations can say whether a setting forecasts well.

7. Judge the forecasts

A straight or flattening forecast describes a model’s assumptions. Its shape alone cannot establish that it predicts better. Reuse the three questions from Session 16 on fitting SES:

Evidence Question it answers What it does not establish
Training SSE Which fitted settings score better on the same training observations? Accuracy on later observations.
Residual diagnostics What patterns remain in the fitted model’s errors? A forecast ranking at the required horizon.
Held-out errors or rolling-origin cross-validation How well do forecasts predict observations excluded from fitting? A universal winner for every series and horizon.

The population fits illustrate how level, slope and damping produce forecasts. They do not provide a held-out comparison. The required internet exercise practices residual diagnostics and interprets the forecast paths; its optional cross-validation extension supplies the additional evidence needed to compare predictive accuracy. Group Assignment 2 also uses held-out evaluation.

Appendix: supporting explanations and variants

The sections below extend the main route. None of them is required, and no new implementation from scratch is needed.

Optional: reconstruct the fitted values

Just as in the Excel workbook, the prior predictions can be computed from the level and slope that components() returns, with the rule \(\hat y_{t|t-1}=\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1}\) from section 4:

# Use the equation for the prior predictions
holts_components <-
  holts_components |>
  mutate(
    .fitted = lag(level) + lag(slope) # Prior prediction: previous level plus slope
  )

They match augment()’s .fitted column, the fitted values in fable’s terms:

# Vector of fitted values computed using augment
fitted_augment <-
  fit_ses_holt |>
    select(Holt) |>
    augment() |>
    pull(.fitted)

# Vector of fitted values computed using the components() and the equation
fitted_components <-
  holts_components |>
  pull(.fitted)

# Remove NAs
fitted_components <-  fitted_components[!is.na(fitted_components)]

all.equal(fitted_augment, fitted_components)
[1] TRUE

The geometric sum behind the damped limit

The damping weights form the same finite geometric sum used for the SES weights in Session 15. Define \(D_h=\phi+\phi^2+\dots+\phi^h\). Multiply by \(\phi\) and subtract; the middle powers cancel:

\[ D_h-\phi D_h=\phi-\phi^{h+1},\qquad D_h=\frac{\phi(1-\phi^h)}{1-\phi}\quad(0<\phi<1). \]

At \(\phi=1\), use the sum itself: \(D_h=h\), giving Holt. Do not substitute that endpoint into the fraction.

For \(0<\phi<1\), \(\phi^h\) shrinks toward zero, so the dimensionless sum tends to \(\phi/(1-\phi)\) as \(h\to\infty\). The forecast \(\ell_T+D_hb_T\) therefore tends to \(\ell_T+\phi b_T/(1-\phi)\), in the units of the series. A rising path approaches that limit from below and a falling one from above.

Reference sketches

Three hand-drawn sketches from earlier versions of this notebook, kept for reference. The main text and the slides carry the same ideas.

The fitted values and forecasts of Holt’s method: each prior prediction is the previous level plus one slope, and the forecasts from \(T\) all use the same final slope.

The change in level over one period is a slope estimate, because the run is one period.

The fitting loop of section 4. Read its initial values for \(\ell_t\) and \(b_t\) as \(\ell_0\) and \(b_0\), and its question “Minimality of SSE satisfied?” as the stopping rule.

Optional: change \(\phi\)’s range

Bounding phi: phi_range gives a lower and an upper bound, and ETS() estimates \(\phi\) within them:

fit_phi_range <-
  aus_economy |>
      model(
        holts = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("N")),

        # Estimate phi between 0.8 and 0.95
        damped_holts = ETS(Pop ~ error("A") +
                                 trend("Ad", phi = NULL, phi_range=c(0.8, 0.95)) +
                                 season("N")
                      )
    )
tidy(fit_phi_range)
# A tibble: 9 × 4
  Country   .model       term  estimate
  <fct>     <chr>        <chr>    <dbl>
1 Australia holts        alpha    1.000
2 Australia holts        beta     0.327
3 Australia holts        l[0]    10.1  
4 Australia holts        b[0]     0.222
5 Australia damped_holts alpha    0.533
6 Australia damped_holts beta     0.533
7 Australia damped_holts phi      0.950
8 Australia damped_holts l[0]     9.96 
9 Australia damped_holts b[0]     0.207

Here \(\phi\) stops at the new upper bound, 0.95, and the other estimates move with it: alpha and beta are both 0.533, so \(\beta^*\) = beta / alpha = 1 and the slope takes up each change in level in full. Changing a bound changes the whole fit, not only \(\phi\).

fc_phi_range <-
  fit_phi_range |>
  forecast(h = 15)

fc_phi_range |>
  autoplot(aus_economy, level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Australian population",
       y = "Millions") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Forecast"))
